displayQuote: If I'm going to sing like someone else, then I don't need to sing at all

meta.title: Who really said "If I'm going to sing like someone else, then I don't need to sing at all"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Widely credited to Billie Holiday, but no primary source pins the wording — Wikiquote has held it unsourced since 2009. What she verifiably did say.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If I'm going to sing like someone else, then I don't need to sing at all'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Billie Holiday everywhere, sourced nowhere. Unsourced on Wikiquote since 2009 — yet the idea is genuinely hers. Here's what she really said.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Credited to Holiday everywhere and entirely of a piece with what she demonstrably believed — she said much the same thing, in her own words, in Lady Sings the Blues and to Willis Conover on the air in 1956. But no primary source pins this wording to her: it has sat in Wikiquote’s unsourced pile since 2009, and the aggregators that spread it cite nothing at all.

source.heading: What the record actually contains
source.excerpt: I can’t stand to sing the same song the same way two nights in succession, let alone two years or ten years. If you can, then it ain’t music, it’s close-order drill or exercise or yodeling or something, not music. […] No two people on earth are alike, and it’s got to be that way in music or it isn’t music.
trail: Quote Investigator has never taken this one up. There is no QI article on the line, so there is no specialist finding to defer to — and no earlier attestation under any other name has ever surfaced.

Wikiquote worked through the memoir and didn’t find it. The article’s Lady Sings the Blues section ↗ cites individual chapters — 4, 11, 17, 20, 22, 23, 24 — and includes her ch. 4 statement that “No two people on earth are alike, and it’s got to be that way in music or it isn’t music.” This quote appears nowhere on the page.

It was demoted to the unsourced pile in 2009 and never rescued. The editor Antiquary moved it to the talk page’s Unsourced list ↗ on 14 August 2009, with an open invitation to restore it given a reliable, precise and verifiable source.

The 1956 broadcast tells the story differently. In Willis Conover’s Music USA interview ↗, recorded 15 February 1956, Holiday says she copied her style from Louis Armstrong, wanted Bessie Smith’s big sound, found it didn’t work because her own voice was small, and out of the compromise “sort of got Billie Holiday.” The transcript records that answer — not this sentence.
source.cutTag: Two separate passages, both cited to ch. 4
source.excerptNote: This is not the quote. It is the closest thing to it that carries a real citation — two passages Wikiquote attributes to chapter 4 ↗ of Lady Sings the Blues. Holiday’s conviction is unmistakable and documented; the fourteen-word version of it is what has no home.

artifact.linkText: Read Willis Conover's Music USA transcript

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted, because no source work has been identified — and an unsourced line is never safe to call public domain. Note that both candidate sources would be in copyright regardless: Lady Sings the Blues was published by Doubleday in 1956, and the Conover interview was recorded the same year, so neither is anywhere near the pre-1931 threshold. Treat the wording as of unknown provenance and unclear rights.

author.name: Billie Holiday
author.kicker: The voice that refused to be anyone else’s
author.heading: Who was Billie Holiday?
author.metaLine: 1915–1959 · American jazz singer, born Eleanora Fagan
author.bio: Born Eleanora Fagan in Philadelphia in 1915, Billie Holiday became the most influential jazz singer of the twentieth century without a day of formal training — she built her style by listening to how horn players phrased, not only to other singers. She told the Voice of America in 1956 that she had wanted Bessie Smith’s big sound and Louis Armstrong’s feeling, found that Smith’s power didn’t suit her small voice, and out of the compromise “sort of got Billie Holiday.” Her 1956 memoir Lady Sings the Blues, ghostwritten by William Dufty, is the source of most of what she is quoted as saying; she died in New York in 1959, aged 44.

cite.sourceCitation: No primary source located for this wording. Nearest documented articulation: Billie Holiday with William Dufty, Lady Sings the Blues (New York: Doubleday, 1956), ch. 4. misattribution.heading: Not the wrong person — the wrong kind of confidence
misattribution.intro: Nobody has ever credibly claimed this line for anyone but Billie Holiday, and this page does not either. The problem is sourcing: it is presented everywhere as a documented quotation, and it has never been documented anywhere.

items.who: BrainyQuote, Goodreads, A-Z Quotes and social media
items.why: The aggregators reproduce the line with a name and nothing else. Goodreads lists no source work at all ↗ and carries a standing notice that its quotes are added by users and not verified.

Her memoir is the natural guess, and some listings assert it. But Wikiquote’s section drawn from that book ↗ cites chapter by chapter through chapters 4, 11, 17, 20, 22, 23 and 24 — and this line is not among them. The book is in copyright and lending-restricted, so it cannot be searched in full to settle the point either way.

The line was stripped from the article to the talk page’s Unsourced list ↗ on 14 August 2009, under a notice inviting anyone to restore it with a reliable, precise and verifiable source. In sixteen years, no one has.

misattribution.truthLine: What Holiday is documented as saying is better than the slogan: “No two people on earth are alike, and it’s got to be that way in music or it isn’t music” — cited to chapter 4 of Lady Sings the Blues ↗. The clause usually quoted alongside it — that copying leaves you “working without any real feeling” — is widely reproduced from the memoir, but Wikiquote does not carry it and no source pins it to a chapter.

context.heading: The idea is hers. The sentence may not be.
lead: This is the unusual case where a quote is almost certainly faithful to its author and still cannot be verified. Holiday built her entire artistic identity on the refusal to imitate other singers, and she said so repeatedly and on the record — in her memoir, in interviews, in the story she told about her own voice. The line circulating under her name compresses that conviction into fourteen crisp words. The trouble is that nobody has ever produced the page or the tape where she said them.

What she actually told Willis Conover in February 1956 ↗ is more interesting than the slogan. Asked where her voice came from, she credited Louis Armstrong’s feeling and Bessie Smith’s sound, then explained that Smith’s big voice simply didn’t fit her — and that somewhere in the compromise between the two, she “sort of got Billie Holiday.” That is not a woman announcing she would rather not sing than sing like someone else. That is a woman describing how she borrowed from two people and ended up sounding like neither.
context.detailsSummary: Why the line probably isn’t a fabrication — just an orphan
detailsBody: Most quotes that go viral under a famous name are fabrications, misattributions, or drift from a different author. This one shows none of those markers. No rival originator has ever surfaced, no earlier printing under another name is known, and the sentiment matches her documented views so closely that a paraphrase of her memoir is the likeliest explanation.

The strongest candidate for what it paraphrases is a passage the aggregators reproduce without a chapter locator — everyone has to be different, you can’t copy anybody and end up with anything — ending in the one sentence Wikiquote pins to chapter 4 ↗ of Lady Sings the Blues: “No two people on earth are alike, and it’s got to be that way in music or it isn’t music.” Turn that into something you can fit on a poster and you get very close to the quote in question.

That remains an observation, not a finding. The 1956 memoir is still in copyright and its scans are lending-restricted, so it cannot be searched end to end from the open web — which is precisely why this page stops at “attributed” rather than declaring the line a paraphrase outright.
context.pull: Holiday didn’t refuse to copy anyone. She copied two people badly enough to become herself.
